question.prompt: Jack wants to bike from his house to Jill’s house, which is located three blocks east and two blocks north of Jack’s house. After biking each block, Jack can continue either east or north, but he needs to avoid a dangerous intersection one block east and one block north of his house. In how many ways can he reach Jill’s house by biking a total of five blocks?

solutions.explanation:
Write \(E\) for one block east and \(N\) for one block north. Every route to Jill's house must contain three \(E\)'s and two \(N\)'s. Jack reaches the dangerous intersection exactly when his first two moves are \(EN\) or \(NE\), since that intersection is one block in each direction from his house.

A safe route must therefore begin with \(EE\) or \(NN\). After \(EE\), Jack is already farther east than the dangerous intersection; after \(NN\), he is already farther north. Because he never moves west or south, all completions of these starts remain safe.

Starting with \(EE\) leaves one \(E\) and two \(N\)'s, which can occur as \(ENN\), \(NEN\), or \(NNE\). This gives three routes. Starting with \(NN\) leaves only \(EEE\), giving one route. These cases cover every safe route and have different starts, so none is counted twice. The total is \(3+1=4\) ways, choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
solutions.title: Examine the first two moves

solutions.explanation:
Write \(E\) for one block east and \(N\) for one block north. Every five-block route to Jill's house contains three \(E\)'s and two \(N\)'s. Count all such routes by choosing the positions of the two northward moves. If the earlier \(N\) is in position \(1,2,3,\) or \(4\), the later \(N\) has \(4,3,2,\) or \(1\) possible positions, respectively. Thus there are
\[
4+3+2+1=10
\]
unrestricted routes. Each route determines exactly one pair of northward positions, so this count has no omissions or repetitions.

A route through the dangerous intersection must reach it after two moves, either \(EN\) or \(NE\). From there, the remaining two eastward moves and one northward move can be ordered as \(EEN\), \(ENE\), or \(NEE\). Each of the two starts has three completions, giving \(2\times3=6\) dangerous routes. Every dangerous route has a unique start and completion, so it is counted once.

Removing these routes leaves \(10-6=4\) safe ways, choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
solutions.title: Subtract the routes through the intersection
